draft.title: Volume of a prism
card: Volume is the amount of space inside a solid. It is measured in cubic units, such as \(\text{cm}^{3}\).

A right prism has the same cross-section all the way along its length. Volume \(=\) area of cross-section \(\times\) length (or height). In symbols, \(V = Ah\), where \(A\) is the area of the cross-section and \(h\) is the length or height of the prism. It works for any prism.
The cross-section is a rectangle, so volume \(=\) length \(\times\) width \(\times\) height.
The cross-section is a triangle. Example: triangle area \(6 \text{ cm}^{2}\) and length 10 cm gives volume \(6 \times 10 = 60 \text{ cm}^{3}\).
draft.remember: For any prism, \(V = Ah\): cross-section area times length or height, in cubic units.

a.q: A prism has a rectangular cross-section 5 cm by 4 cm. It is 3 cm high. What is its volume?
a.why: The cross-section area is \(5 \times 4 = 20 \text{ cm}^{2}\). Then \(V = Ah = 20 \times 3 = 60 \text{ cm}^{3}\). Adding the lengths to get 12 is a common mistake, but volume needs multiplying.

b.q: A triangular prism has an end of area \(2 \text{ m}^{2}\) and a length of 3 m. Use \(V = Ah\) to find its volume.
b.why: The triangular end is the cross-section, so \(A = 2\) and \(h = 3\). Then \(V = 2 \times 3 = 6 \text{ m}^{3}\). Adding 2 and 3 gives 5, which is not how volume works.
b.clue: The triangle's area is already worked out.
